name: Blockchain & Smart Contract Security
description: Security of blockchains, consensus, cryptocurrencies, DeFi, and smart contracts.

uss.narrative:
The earliest USENIX Security papers in this area (2018) were grappling with two foundational tensions of programmable blockchains. On one side, "Arbitrum: Scalable, private smart contracts" (USENIX 2018) tackled the systems-level limits of Ethereum-style contracts, proposing a way to run them with better scalability and privacy. On the other, "teEther: Gnawing at Ethereum to Automatically Exploit Smart Contracts" (USENIX 2018) showed that deployed contracts were riddled with bugs that could be found and exploited automatically, while "An Empirical Analysis of Anonymity in Zcash" (USENIX 2018) demonstrated that even privacy-focused coins leaked deanonymizing patterns. From the very start the field split into smart-contract security, consensus/network security, and cryptocurrency privacy.

Through 2019-2021 the dominant thread became ever more sophisticated smart-contract analysis and a growing appreciation that real-world ecosystems behave differently than toy threat models. Work moved from finding bugs in isolation toward understanding adversarial economics: "The Art of The Scam" (USENIX 2019) dissected honeypot contracts designed to trick attackers, and "Frontrunner Jones and the Raiders of the Dark Forest" (USENIX 2021) gave the first large empirical picture of frontrunning, foreshadowing the MEV agenda. Analysis tooling matured with bounded model checking in "ETHBMC" (USENIX 2020), transaction-trace forensics in "TXSPECTOR" (USENIX 2020), and language-model-guided symbolic execution in "SmarTest" (USENIX 2021). Crucially, "Smart Contract Vulnerabilities: Vulnerable Does Not Imply Exploited" (USENIX 2021) reframed the field by showing that most flagged vulnerabilities were never actually exploited, pushing researchers toward exploitability rather than mere presence of bugs.

By 2022-2023 the work broadened beyond Ethereum and beyond static vulnerability hunting. New platforms were scrutinized in "EOSAFE" (USENIX 2021) and "Panda: Security Analysis of Algorand Smart Contracts" (USENIX 2023); consensus itself advanced with asynchronous BFT in "WaterBear" (USENIX 2023). The DeFi economy became a first-class object of study with "A Large Scale Study of the Ethereum Arbitrage Ecosystem" (USENIX 2023) and cross-chain light clients in "Glimpse" (USENIX 2023), while "Proxy Hunting" (USENIX 2023) exposed the security cost of upgradeable contracts. The community also turned reflexively on its own assumptions, studying developers themselves in "A Mixed-Methods Study of Security Practices of Smart Contract Developers" (USENIX 2023) and user privacy in "Is Your Wallet Snitching On You?" (USENIX 2023), alongside ML-based detection in "Smart Learning to Find Dumb Contracts" (USENIX 2023).

Most recently the frontier has shifted toward active defense and multi-chain interoperability. "Your Exploit is Mine: Instantly Synthesizing Counterattack Smart Contract" (USENIX 2023) turned exploitation techniques into a defensive weapon by auto-generating counterattacks, and "Parallelizing Universal Atomic Swaps for Multi-Chain Cryptocurrency Exchanges" (USENIX 2025) reflects the field's move into trustless cross-chain exchange as the cryptocurrency landscape fragments across many ledgers. Taken together, the area has evolved from "can we find a bug in a contract" to "how do entire decentralized financial systems, their networks, their developers, and their cross-chain plumbing fail and defend themselves."

ndss.narrative:
The earliest NDSS work in this list wrestled with two foundational problems: making smart contracts safe and making blockchains scale. On the safety side, "ZEUS: Analyzing Safety of Smart Contracts" (NDSS 2018) framed the core anxiety of the space — a buggy contract cannot be patched once it holds real money — and applied formal verification to catch defects before deployment. In parallel, "Chainspace: A Sharded Smart Contracts Platform" (NDSS 2018) and "Settling Payments Fast and Private" (NDSS 2018) attacked throughput, the former through sharding and the latter through private off-chain payment routing, setting up the scalability thread that runs through the whole decade.

Through 2019 and 2020 the field split into clearer sub-tracks. Layer-2 and payment-channel research matured with "Anonymous Multi-Hop Locks for Blockchain Scalability and Interoperability" (NDSS 2019), which became a widely-cited building block for secure channel networks. Consensus and cryptocurrency design got sharper with "Vault: Fast Bootstrapping for the Algorand Cryptocurrency" (NDSS 2019) and "Bobtail: Improved Blockchain Security with Low-Variance Mining" (NDSS 2020). At the same time contract-security tooling moved from static verification toward runtime and online detection, exemplified by "SODA: A Generic Online Detection Framework for Smart Contracts" (NDSS 2020), reflecting a growing recognition that attackers were actively hunting lucrative contracts in the wild.

The 2021-2023 period is where the field's methods diversified and the adversary got smarter on both sides. "SquirRL: Automating Attack Analysis on Blockchain Incentive Mechanisms with Deep Reinforcement Learning" (NDSS 2021) showed automated agents discovering attacks on incentive mechanisms, and "LOKI: State-Aware Fuzzing Framework for the Implementation of Blockchain Consensus Protocols" (NDSS 2023) pushed fuzzing into consensus implementations. Detection turned to machine learning with "Smarter Contracts: Detecting Vulnerabilities in Smart Contracts with Deep Transfer Learning" (NDSS 2023), while network-layer threats surfaced in "Partitioning Ethereum without Eclipsing It" (NDSS 2023). A notable shift is the appearance of ecosystem-and-fraud research — "Double and Nothing: Understanding and Detecting Cryptocurrency Giveaway Scams" (NDSS 2023) — signaling that the community had begun treating scams and user-facing abuse as first-class security problems alongside protocol flaws.

By 2024-2026 the area has matured into several parallel frontiers. Smart-contract analysis grew more specialized, from "Not your Type! Detecting Storage Collision Vulnerabilities in Ethereum Smart Contracts" (NDSS 2024) to "Silence False Alarms: Identifying Anti-Reentrancy Patterns" (NDSS 2025), which tackles the false-positive problem in reentrancy detection rather than reentrancy itself. Zero-knowledge tooling became a target of its own in "MTZK: Testing and Exploring Bugs in Zero-Knowledge (ZK) Compilers" (NDSS 2025). The very latest 2026 papers show the field's current center of gravity: DeFi economic security and MEV are now central, with "Light into Darkness: Demystifying Profit Strategies Throughout the MEV Bot Lifecycle" and "MEVisor: High-Throughput MEV Discovery in DEXs with GPU Parallelism"; asynchronous BFT consensus is being refined for practicality in "Ipotane: Balancing the Good and Bad Cases of Asynchronous BFT" and "Icarus: Achieving Performant Asynchronous BFT with Only Optimistic Paths"; incentive-layer flaws are hunted automatically by "BunnyFinder: Finding Incentive Flaws for Ethereum Consensus"; and user-facing crime remains prominent through "Phishing in Wonderland: Evaluating Learning-Based Ethereum Phishing Transaction Detection and Pitfalls" and "CtPhishCapture: Uncovering Credential-Theft-Based Phishing Scams Targeting Cryptocurrency Wallets." The trajectory is clear: from patching individual contracts, through scaling and consensus, to a broad discipline covering economic attacks, protocol internals, and protecting ordinary crypto users.

sp.narrative:
The earliest work in this list, all from IEEE S&P 2018, wrestled with the two problems that dominated early blockchain research: privacy and scale. "Bulletproofs: Short Proofs for Confidential Transactions and More" (S&P 2018) gave a compact non-interactive zero-knowledge proof that made confidential transaction amounts practical, and it became one of the most-cited results in the whole area. Alongside it, "OmniLedger: A Secure, Scale-Out, Decentralized Ledger via Sharding" (S&P 2018) attacked throughput by splitting the ledger into shards, while "Tracking Ransomware End-to-end" (S&P 2018) showed the maturing side of the field — measuring how cryptocurrency actually moves through the criminal economy.

Around 2019-2020 the research spread outward into layer-2 systems, interoperability, and consensus. Payment channels and cross-chain bridges appear in "Perun: Virtual Payment Hubs over Cryptocurrencies" (S&P 2019), "XCLAIM: Trustless, Interoperable, Cryptocurrency-Backed Assets" (S&P 2019), and "Proof-of-Stake Sidechains" (S&P 2019), while consensus theory sharpened with "Sync HotStuff" (S&P 2020) and "OHIE: Blockchain Scaling Made Simple" (S&P 2020). In parallel a program-analysis subfield emerged to cope with buggy smart contracts, producing "VerX: Safety Verification of Smart Contracts" (S&P 2020) and "VERISMART: A Highly Precise Safety Verifier for Ethereum Smart Contracts" (S&P 2020).

The defining shift arrived with the rise of DeFi and the discovery that the ordering of transactions is itself an attack surface. "Flash Boys 2.0" (S&P 2020) named miner-extractable value and consensus instability, "High-Frequency Trading on Decentralized On-Chain Exchanges" (S&P 2021) and "On the Just-In-Time Discovery of Profit-Generating Transactions in DeFi Protocols" (S&P 2021) turned it into a concrete threat, and "Quantifying Blockchain Extractable Value: How dark is the forest?" (S&P 2022) measured its true scale. This economic-security lens matured into formal and systematizing work such as "Clockwork Finance: Automated Analysis of Economic Security in Smart Contracts" (S&P 2023) and "SoK: Decentralized Finance (DeFi) Attacks" (S&P 2023), while "SoK: Security and Privacy of Blockchain Interoperability" (S&P 2024) consolidated the cross-chain thread that XCLAIM had opened years earlier.

The most recent papers, from S&P 2026, show the field converging on hard cryptographic and consensus guarantees rather than one-off attacks. Mempool-ordering fairness — the descendant of the MEV line — is now tackled cryptographically in "Weighted Batched Threshold Encryption With Applications to Mempool Privacy" (S&P 2026), and privacy has grown from Bulletproofs' hidden amounts into full "Jigsaw: Doubly Private Smart Contracts" (S&P 2026). Consensus work is now heavily verification-driven, with "Mechanized Safety and Liveness Proofs for the Mysticeti Consensus Protocol" (S&P 2026) and the offensive counterpart "A Liveness Attack to Ethereum PoS with No Additional Cost" (S&P 2026), while tooling has followed the technology stack into zero-knowledge circuits themselves with "zkFuzz: Foundation and Framework for Effective Fuzzing of Zero-Knowledge Circuits" (S&P 2026).

ccs.narrative:
Blockchain security at CCS encompasses smart contract analysis, consensus protocol design, and ecosystem measurement. The 2018 landmark papers arrived together: Securify: Practical Security Analysis of Smart Contracts (CCS 2018) gave the community its most-cited automated contract verifier, while RapidChain: Scaling Blockchain via Full Sharding (CCS 2018) set a throughput record via full protocol sharding. Consensus protocol foundations came from BEAT: Asynchronous BFT Made Practical (CCS 2018) and off-chain scaling from General State Channel Networks (CCS 2018).

The 2019 cohort expanded in scope. Prism: Deconstructing the Blockchain to Approach Physical Limits (CCS 2019) separated the confirmation and transaction roles of blocks to approach network-speed throughput. Learning to Fuzz from Symbolic Execution with Application to Smart Contracts (CCS 2019) brought fuzzing to contract vulnerability discovery, and MatRiCT: Efficient, Scalable and Post-Quantum Blockchain Confidential Transactions Protocol (CCS 2019) introduced lattice-based privacy for blockchain payments.

By 2021-2022, DeFi and cross-chain infrastructure became primary concerns. Bullshark: DAG BFT Protocols Made Practical (CCS 2022) demonstrated DAG-based consensus at scale, zkBridge: Trustless Cross-chain Bridges Made Practical (CCS 2022) enabled ZK-verified state relay between chains, and Understanding Security Issues in the NFT Ecosystem (CCS 2022) exposed the fraud and scam surface of NFT markets. EIP-1559 was empirically evaluated in Empirical Analysis of EIP-1559 (CCS 2022).

top4.narrative:
The earliest work on this list, from 2018, splits cleanly along two fault lines that still define the field. On one side sit the scalability and consensus builders: "OmniLedger: A Secure, Scale-Out, Decentralized Ledger via Sharding" (S&P 2018) and "RapidChain: Scaling Blockchain via Full Sharding" (CCS 2018) attacked the throughput ceiling of permissionless ledgers by partitioning state across shards, while "BEAT: Asynchronous BFT Made Practical" (CCS 2018) pushed Byzantine agreement toward real deployment. On the other side sit the smart-contract auditors, reacting to the fact that buggy Ethereum contracts hold real money and cannot be patched: "ZEUS: Analyzing Safety of Smart Contracts" (NDSS 2018), "Securify: Practical Security Analysis of Smart Contracts" (CCS 2018), and "teEther: Gnawing at Ethereum to Automatically Exploit Smart Contracts" (USENIX 2018) built static analysis and automated exploit generation for contract bugs. Cryptographic plumbing landed the same year, most influentially "Bulletproofs: Short Proofs for Confidential Transactions and More" (S&P 2018), whose short zero-knowledge range proofs became infrastructure for confidential transactions everywhere.

Around 2019 the emphasis shifted from single chains to moving value between and off of them. A wave of layer-2 and interoperability designs appeared: "Perun: Virtual Payment Hubs over Cryptocurrencies" (S&P 2019) and "Anonymous Multi-Hop Locks for Blockchain Scalability and Interoperability" (NDSS 2019) advanced payment channels, while "XCLAIM: Trustless, Interoperable, Cryptocurrency-Backed Assets" (S&P 2019) and "Proof-of-Stake Sidechains" (S&P 2019) tackled cross-chain assets. Threshold cryptography for wallet custody also matured, with "Threshold ECDSA from ECDSA Assumptions: The Multiparty Case" (S&P 2019) building on the earlier "Fast Secure Multiparty ECDSA" (CCS 2018). Meanwhile contract analysis kept getting smarter, blending fuzzing with symbolic execution in "Learning to Fuzz from Symbolic Execution with Application to Smart Contracts" (CCS 2019), and empirical work like "The Art of The Scam: Demystifying Honeypots in Ethereum Smart Contracts" (USENIX 2019) began measuring how attackers actually behave in the wild.

The defining conceptual breakthrough arrived with "Flash Boys 2.0: Frontrunning in Decentralized Exchanges, Miner Extractable Value, and Consensus Instability" (S&P 2020), which named miner/maximal extractable value (MEV) and showed that ordering transactions is itself an exploitable resource that can destabilize consensus. This reframed a huge slice of subsequent research: "High-Frequency Trading on Decentralized On-Chain Exchanges" (S&P 2021), "Frontrunner Jones and the Raiders of the Dark Forest" (USENIX 2021), and "Quantifying Blockchain Extractable Value: How dark is the forest?" (S&P 2022) turned MEV from a concept into a measured, quantified phenomenon. In parallel, verification grew more ambitious with "VerX: Safety Verification of Smart Contracts" (S&P 2020) proving functional properties rather than just spotting bug patterns, privacy computation advanced through "ZEXE: Enabling Decentralized Private Computation" (S&P 2020), and consensus kept improving via "Sync HotStuff" (S&P 2020) and later the DAG-based "Bullshark: DAG BFT Protocols Made Practical" (CCS 2022). The ecosystem also broadened outward, with "Understanding Security Issues in the NFT Ecosystem" (CCS 2022) and "zkBridge: Trustless Cross-chain Bridges Made Practical" (CCS 2022) reflecting the DeFi and cross-chain boom.

The most recent work, clustered at NDSS 2026, shows a field that has matured into distinct, deepening specialties rather than chasing one big idea. Consensus research is thriving and increasingly nuanced, with "Ipotane: Balancing the Good and Bad Cases of Asynchronous BFT" and "Icarus: Achieving Performant Asynchronous BFT with Only Optimistic Paths" refining the asynchronous BFT designs that BEAT started, "Pallas and Aegis: Rollback Resilience in TEE-Aided Blockchain Consensus" folding trusted hardware into agreement, and "BunnyFinder: Finding Incentive Flaws for Ethereum Consensus" and "Mobius: Enabling Byzantine-Resilient Single Secret Leader Election" probing incentive and leader-election weaknesses. MEV research has become an engineering discipline, with "MEVisor: High-Throughput MEV Discovery in DEXs with GPU Parallelism" throwing parallel hardware at extraction discovery. And a strong empirical, user-protection thread now dominates the applied side: "Phishing in Wonderland: Evaluating Learning-Based Ethereum Phishing Transaction Detection and Pitfalls" and "CtPhishCapture: Uncovering Credential-Theft-Based Phishing Scams Targeting Cryptocurrency Wallets" confront the reality that, with the cryptography and contracts hardened, the softest target is now the ordinary user being phished.
